title: Why Houses Became Unaffordable (And Who's Buying Them)
sources: NAR Existing-Home Sales, August 2026 (released Sept 10, 2026): median existing-home price $429,100 (+1.6% YoY, 38th straight monthly YoY gain); inventory 1.62M, 4.9 months' supply; individual investors/second-home buyers 15% of sales; all-cash 27%
U.S. Census Bureau, Income in the United States: 2025 (Sept 15, 2026): median household income $87,460

1995 comparison: NAR median existing-home price ≈ $110,500 (1995 annual); Census CPS ASEC Table H-5 median household income 1995 = $34,076 (current dollars). Ratio 110,500 ÷ 34,076 ≈ 3.2; 2026: 429,100 ÷ 87,460 ≈ 4.9
Freddie Mac PMMS, Sept 24, 2026: 30-year fixed 7.03% (year ago 6.30%); 1995 annual average ≈ 7.9%

Payment math (principal + interest, 20% down, 30 years): 1995 $88,400 at 7.93% ≈ $644/mo ≈ 23% of $2,840 monthly median income; 2026 $343,280 at 7.03% ≈ $2,291/mo ≈ 31% of $7,288 monthly median income. Down payment 20%: $22,100 (0.65 yr income) vs $85,820 (≈1 yr income)
FHFA National Mortgage Database via Redfin (Sept 29, 2025, Q2 2025 data): 52.5% of mortgaged homeowners have a rate below 4%, down from a record 65.1% in 2022
Up for Growth, Housing Underproduction in the U.S. 2025 (Nov 24, 2025): 3.78 million homes underproduced (2023 data); Freddie Mac estimate ≈ 3.7 million (2024)
NAHB (2021): regulation accounts for ≈ 23.8% of the price of a new single-family home
Institutional investors: GAO-24-106643 (2024) and Urban Institute: large investors (1,000+ homes) own roughly 3% of single-family rental homes nationally, but about one in four in metro Atlanta
NAR 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers (Nov 2025): first-time buyer share record low 21%, median first-time buyer age record high 40 (29 in 1981)

youtube.title: Why Houses Became Unaffordable (And Who's Buying Them)
alt_titles: Houses Cost 5 Years of Income Now. Here's Why.
Is Wall Street Buying All the Houses? Housing Crisis Explained
youtube.hook: Why are houses so unaffordable? In 1995 a home cost ~3 years of income. Today it's almost 5. Here's what changed, and who's really buying. Dave's dad bought a house in 1995 on one salary. Dave and his partner can't, even with two. We compare home prices and incomes then and now (NAR, Census), explain why 7% mortgage rates hurt so much, how cheap pandemic mortgages created the lock-in effect, why America is short about 3.7 to 3.8 million homes, how zoning, permits and building costs slow construction, how much Wall Street investors really own (small nationally, big in Atlanta), and why the typical first-time buyer is now 40. This is the final episode of Series 3.

beats.text: This is my dad's house. He bought it in nineteen ninety five with one salary and two kids and a dog named Biscuit.
This is me and my girlfriend. Two salaries. Both full time. And we can't afford the garage.
My dad paid about three years of his pay for that house. The same house today costs about five years.
And the average person buying their first home in America is now forty. Forty.
By the end of this video you'll know who's really buying all the houses and I promise it's not who you think.
But most people scroll away before that part which is exactly how they end up renting forever.
So let me show you the ruler I use now. How many years of pay does a house cost?
When my dad bought his house it cost him about three years of pay. You could save for that. You could actually see the finish line.
Back then a guy with a normal job could buy a house and a car and still take the family to the beach every summer.
Today the typical home is about five years of pay. And that's if you spend nothing. No food. No rent. No phone. Just vibes.
Me trying to save five years of pay while also paying rent and eating food like a normal person.
It's like a ladder. Our pay climbed a few steps. House prices took the elevator.
My paycheck trying to catch up with house prices.
And it gets worse. Nobody pays cash for a house. You borrow. And borrowing got expensive.
Mortgage rates are around seven percent now. A few years ago they were three.
Three to seven doesn't sound like much. But on a loan that big it's the difference between a car payment and a second rent.
My dad paid even higher rates than that. Sounds worse right? But he borrowed way less money. So his monthly payment was tiny.
My payment on a normal house today? About two thousand three hundred dollars a month. Before taxes. Before insurance. Before the roof leaks.
Two thousand three hundred a month. That's more than my rent. And my rent already makes me cry in the shower.
Me looking at the monthly payment.
And the down payment? For my dad it was a few months of pay. For me it's a whole year. A whole year of not eating avocado toast.
And yes before you comment. I stopped buying avocado toast. I'm now twelve dollars closer to a house.
I did the math. At twelve dollars a week I'll have my down payment in about a hundred and fifty years.
So I start looking for a house anyway. And the first thing I notice? There's almost nothing for sale.
Here's why. A few years ago rates dropped to around three percent and millions of people locked in super cheap loans.
Imagine having a three percent loan. That's like owning a time machine back to cheap money. You don't give that up.
Now imagine you're one of them. If you sell and buy a new house you swap your cheap loan for an expensive one. Your payment jumps overnight.
So people stay put. Kids move out. The house is way too big. They stay anyway. Economists call it the lock in effect.
It's like golden handcuffs. Shiny. Comfy. And you can't leave.
My neighbor with a three percent mortgage and four empty bedrooms.
Older couples in four bedroom houses. Young families in one bedroom apartments. Everyone stuck in the wrong size.
And the other big reason is simple. America didn't build enough homes.
After the crash in two thousand eight builders went bust. For about ten years almost nobody was building.
Meanwhile my whole generation grew up and wanted a place. Lots of new people. Not enough new houses.
My friend Mike and his wife looked at forty houses last year. Forty. They lost every single one to someone with more cash.
It's musical chairs. Ten people. Eight chairs. When the music stops everyone fights for a chair and the chairs get very expensive.
Me playing musical chairs with a guy who already has three chairs.
And building more isn't easy. In a lot of cities the rules only allow one big house on one big lot. No apartments. No townhouses.
Getting a permit can take years. And neighbors show up to meetings and say build it. Just not here.
Every neighbor at the town meeting.
Builders say all those rules add about a quarter to the price of a new home. Before they even buy a single brick.
And lumber and workers and land all got more expensive. So when builders do build they build big fancy houses because those pay more.
Builders deciding what to build.
Okay. The big question. Is Wall Street buying all the houses?
Most people think yes. Nope. Across the whole country the giant investors own only a tiny slice of the homes.
It's like blaming the guy with the biggest cart for the long line at the grocery store. He's annoying but he's not the whole line.
But here's the twist. They don't spread out. They pile into a few fast growing cities. Like Atlanta.
In some Atlanta neighborhoods big investors own about one out of every four rental houses. There they really do compete with families like mine.
Picture a family showing up to an open house with a sandwich and a dream. And a company showing up with a check.
Me bidding against a company with a billion dollars.

beats.text: And there's another buyer. Regular people buying a second house to rent it out. Your dentist. Your uncle. That guy from the gym.
Your dentist owning three houses is honestly more common than a giant fund owning yours.
So who is really buying the houses? Mostly nobody. Because the people who own them aren't selling and the new ones never got built.
That's the answer. It's not one villain in a suit. It's a traffic jam.
And that's why the first time buyer is now forty. When my grandpa bought his first house he was in his twenties.
Forty. At forty my dad was already halfway done paying off his house. I'm just getting started. Maybe.
The people who already own homes watched their prices go up and up. They win. The people trying to get in pay more.
My dad got his first house at twenty eight. I'm thirty four. Still renting. With a cat who also has no equity.
My cat when I say we're moving again.
Me at family dinner when my uncle says just stop buying coffee.
So what am I actually doing about it? Quick reminder this is education and not advice.
First. Renting is not throwing money away. If you might move in a few years renting is often the smarter move.
Renting means when the water heater explodes it's my landlord's problem. I sleep like a baby.
Second. I look at the whole monthly cost. Not just the price. Taxes. Insurance. Repairs. The house is just the beginning.
Third. I check first time buyer programs. Lots of states and cities help with the down payment. Most people never even ask.
Some programs give you thousands toward a down payment and people just don't know they exist. Five minutes of googling. Thousands of dollars.
Fourth. I compare lenders. A tiny difference in the rate can save thousands over the loan.
And fifth. Nobody rushes me. Not the agent. Not my mom. Not the guy on the internet saying buy now or be poor forever.
Real estate agents when I say I'm gonna wait.
So who's buying all the houses? Mostly nobody. The market is stuck. And when it's stuck the people already inside win.
It's not my fault I can't afford my dad's house. And it's not yours either. The math changed.
My dad didn't beat the game because he was smarter. He just played it on easy mode.
But knowing the math means nobody can rush you into the worst deal of your life.
Next time I get paid on Friday and I'm broke by Monday. We'll find out where my paycheck goes.
Subscribe. It's free and unlike a house it will never cost you five years of pay.
